output.summary: In acute vestibular syndrome, a normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation each point to a central cause, and CT is insensitive to posterior fossa ischemia. Lateral medullary infarction is most often due to vertebral artery disease, including dissection. In extracranial cervical artery dissection, antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy have not been shown to differ, and either is reasonable for at least 3 months; the trial evidence does not cover intracranial dissection.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose peripheral vestibular neuritis or BPPV and discharge: crossed sensory findings, Horner syndrome, dysphagia and a central HINTS pattern exclude a peripheral vestibular cause.
Do not rely on a normal CT scan to exclude posterior fossa ischemic stroke: CT is frequently negative in the posterior fossa because of beam-hardening artifact; MRI DWI is the definitive modality.
Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy in the first 24 hours after IV thrombolysis, before follow-up imaging excludes hemorrhage.
Do not withhold IV thrombolysis because of the extracranial vertebral artery dissection or the recent chiropractic manipulation: neither is a contraindication.
Do not delay vessel imaging in posterior circulation stroke: the vertebral artery dissection and its extent must be characterized urgently.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (sudden onset at breakfast, about 2 hours before arrival) and the NIHSS (4: limb ataxia 2, sensory 1, dysarthria 1). The inability to walk and the dysphagia are not scored but make the deficit disabling.
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision.

Recognize the lateral medullary syndrome: crossed pain and temperature loss (right face, left body), right Horner syndrome, hoarseness and dysphagia, right limb ataxia and a central HINTS pattern (normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation); do not attribute it to a peripheral vestibular disorder.

Obtain CTA of the head and neck to characterize the right vertebral artery dissection suggested by the chiropractic cervical manipulation 36 hours earlier, and to exclude intradural extension and basilar occlusion.

IV thrombolysis: give (about 2 hours from last known well; the deficit is disabling despite NIHSS 4: dysphagia to his own saliva, marked dysmetria of the right arm and a gait he cannot manage without falling; CT without hemorrhage; BP 172/96 mmHg, below 185/110; glucose 108 mg/dL, platelets 224, INR 1.0; aspirin use is not a contraindication; the right vertebral dissection is extracranial (V3) without intracranial extension, which is not a contraindication). Thrombectomy: not indicated (no large vessel occlusion; basilar and left vertebral arteries patent).

Give alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) with a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes; blood pressure needs no lowering beforehand, and keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after.
Watch for orolingual angioedema during and after the thrombolytic infusion: he takes lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor.
Confirm the posterior fossa infarct with MRI DWI, which a normal CT does not exclude, without delaying thrombolysis.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours, with post-thrombolysis neurological and blood pressure checks.
Keep him nil by mouth until a formal swallowing assessment (dysphagia to saliva, diminished right gag): high aspiration risk.

After imaging at 24 hours excludes hemorrhage, start antithrombotic therapy for the extracranial vertebral dissection for at least 3 months: single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel) or anticoagulation; CADISS found no difference between them (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention, COR 2a).
Repeat non-invasive vessel imaging (CTA or MRA) at 3 to 6 months to assess healing and decide the duration of antithrombotic therapy; advise against further cervical manipulation.

Treat vascular risk factors: increase atorvastatin to 80 mg (LDL 128 mg/dL on 20 mg; AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention) and resume lisinopril once swallowing is safe and the acute phase is over, with a long-term blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg.

differential.key_features: Vertigo and nausea could mimic peripheral vestibular disease, but the head impulse test is normal, the nystagmus changes direction, there is skew deviation, and crossed sensory loss, Horner syndrome and dysphagia localize to the lateral medulla, where DWI shows the infarct; Dix-Hallpike is negative.

Shares the right vertebral/PICA supply with the lateral medulla and explains ataxia and vertigo, but not crossed sensory loss, Horner syndrome or dysphagia; MRI shows no cerebellar infarct. Extension remains possible while the right PICA fills poorly.

differential.key_features: He has vascular risk factors, but CTA and MRI show a crescentic intramural hematoma at V3 after neck manipulation, with no atherosclerotic plaque at the vertebral origins: dissection, not atheroma.
Acute vascular-territory DWI-positive lesion in a patient without prior demyelinating disease; single lesion in a vascular distribution is atypical for MS
CT and MRI show no hemorrhage in the posterior fossa.

key_clinical_evidence: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome produces a crossed sensory pattern: ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract) and contralateral body/limb pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic tract), localizing to the lateral medulla.

Additional ipsilateral signs of Wallenberg syndrome: Horner syndrome (descending sympathetic fibers), limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), and vertigo with nystagmus (vestibular nuclei).
Corticospinal tracts are spared in the lateral medulla: no limb weakness distinguishes it from pontine or medial medullary strokes.
NIHSS is 4 (limb ataxia 2, sensory 1, dysarthria 1). Gait ataxia and dysphagia are not scored, so the low score understates a disabling deficit.

HINTS here is central on all three components: normal head impulse (no corrective saccade), direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation (Kattah 2009). A positive head impulse with a corrective saccade would be the peripheral pattern.
CT is frequently negative for posterior fossa ischemia because of beam-hardening artifact at the skull base; a normal CT does not exclude brainstem or cerebellar infarction, and MRI DWI confirms it.

IV thrombolysis is given: about 2 hours from last known well, disabling deficit, no hemorrhage, BP 172/96 mmHg, normal glucose, platelets and INR. Extracranial (V3) vertebral dissection without intracranial extension is not a contraindication; no large vessel occlusion, so no thrombectomy.
Right vertebral artery dissection after chiropractic cervical manipulation is the mechanism; the crescentic intramural hematoma on CTA and fat-saturated T1 MRI is the diagnostic hallmark.

For extracranial cervical artery dissection, antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for at least 3 months is reasonable (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention, COR 2a); CADISS found no difference between them. It starts after the 24-hour post-thrombolysis imaging.
Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor: watch for orolingual angioedema during thrombolysis.
Only glucose had to be known before thrombolysis here (no anticoagulant, no suspected coagulopathy); ECG and troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA does not wait for creatinine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Halvorsen is a 58-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia who presents to the emergency department via EMS with acute onset severe vertigo, nausea, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing beginning approximately 2 hours prior to arrival. The patient reports he was eating breakfast at home when he suddenly experienced intense room-spinning dizziness with nausea and one episode of vomiting. He stood up and immediately lurched to the right, grasping the counter. His wife noted he sounded hoarse and was coughing when trying to drink water. He also complained of a sharp, burning pain on the right side of his face. He called 911. There was no preceding headache, visual changes, limb weakness, or loss of consciousness. He denies any hearing loss or ear fullness. He did not notice numbness or weakness in his arms or legs, though his wife reports he appeared clumsy when trying to reach for his phone. Of note, he underwent chiropractic cervical manipulation approximately 36 hours prior for intermittent neck stiffness and soreness, a treatment he had received on two prior occasions without incident. On initial evaluation in the emergency department, the treating physician noted the patient's prominent dizziness and nausea and initially considered a peripheral vestibular disorder such as vestibular neuritis or BPPV. Neurology was urgently consulted. Time from symptom onset to ED presentation: approximately 2 hours. Last known well: 2 hours prior to arrival.
